# The *diagnosis*.

::: callout-important
## In Brief

This chapter is a diagnostic. You'll name what's actually broken in your company's AI approach. It's not the tools, the training, or the team. It's the operating model. By the end you'll have scored your business on a twenty-question AI Readiness Scorecard, you'll have a single percentage that puts you on one side of the AI divide or the other, and you'll know which of five dimensions to start with.
:::

We learned most of it from one question.

We were on a discovery call with a long-time client, a mid-size manufacturing company, about fifty people, eight-figure revenue. The CEO and two of his direct reports were on the screen. We asked how they were using AI. The CEO said ChatGPT. One director said Claude. The other said Poe, an aggregator that lets you sample models without committing to one.

Three people. One company. Three different tools. No shared accounts or projects, no shared workflow. Each of them had gone out and found something on their own, the same way someone downloads a new app to try it out. And each of them was using it the same way: individually, occasionally, for whatever felt useful in the moment.

We asked what they were hoping AI would do for the business. The answer was honest: they had a gut sense that AI could be doing more for the company, but they didn't know what was even possible. They booked the call precisely because they didn't know what they wanted, only that they were leaving something on the table.

This is a design problem. It's the most common version of the AI problem we see: three people using three tools, with no coordination and no structural change. No one designed the work before the tool arrived.

The design we mean is the *operating model*: how work actually moves through your company. Who decides what gets done, who hands what to whom, what each function is accountable for. The org chart names the boxes. The operating model is how work moves between them.

We've watched this same pattern for two decades, long before AI entered the conversation. A mid-market company would complete an acquisition and absorb the new entity without redesigning how work actually moved. The acquired operation got bolted onto the existing structure, with the same managers handling expanded volume. The accountability map was never rebuilt to match the expanded scope. AI is just the latest technology to expose a problem that's been visible the whole time.

Raffaella Sadun, in *Harvard Business Review* (August 2023), called out the pattern directly: "vast differences in the extent to which some firms are really able to click and figure out how to use these technologies for their own benefit," opening "between those that are at the frontier and those that remain behind." Only 5% of AI implementations deliver measurable business returns, per the MIT study cited by AWS and Effectual in *Harvard Business Review* (June 2026). The scorecard at the close of this chapter is the diagnostic that tells you where your company stands.

This pattern is common. It might describe your company.

> You know AI matters. You just don't know what it can actually do inside your company — or where to start.

That sentence isn't a secret. CEOs say it all the time: to their boards, their coaches, their peers at dinner. They know AI matters, they've started looking, and they still can't find the entry point that makes sense for the business they run. We've watched this happen inside our own companies and inside the companies we work with. Agents are doing real work. Smaller teams are shipping more. The cost curve of knowledge work is bending in ways that no longer feel theoretical. The gap is between that reality and what you're supposed to *do* about it inside the company you run.

It's not for lack of effort. You bought subscriptions, ran a pilot or two, brought in a consultant, sat through a vendor demo. What you've got to show for it is a tool your team barely uses and a handful of use cases that never scaled. The missing piece is how to design the work.

We were on a call with a company that runs on EOS (the Entrepreneurial Operating System): Accountability Chart, scorecards, L10 meetings, the works. A disciplined company. And even here, they couldn't frame the AI problem, let alone implement a solution. They had AI subscriptions across the team. One marketing lead was building an agent in Microsoft Copilot on her own time, after hours. Everyone else was using AI as a sounding board. No workflow had changed. No output was different. When we asked who in the organization could drive their AI initiative, the owner paused and said four words: "I don't have that person."

One person working harder inside a system that was never designed for AI doesn't move the company.

The instinct is to blame adoption, or to blame the tool itself. *AI can't do X. It's not ready for our industry.* That diagnosis is comfortable because it avoids fixing the operating model. Acting on it produces exactly one outcome: another training session that also doesn't work.

The real problem is upstream of adoption, and it has two parts. The first: the company has no designed structure for a non-human worker to operate inside. Nobody built that before the AI subscriptions started. The second is just as common and rarely named. Operators don't yet have a clear picture of what AI can actually do inside a business like theirs. They've seen the demos. They've read the headlines. They haven't seen what a designed agent workflow looks like in their own operation, with their own data, hitting their own numbers. So the asks stay small, and the design conversation never starts.

To use AI, non-technical and bricks-and-mortar businesses have to learn structures software companies have used for years: workflows run as systems, knowledge stored as an indexed asset, handoffs built as interfaces. That means new terms and new processes. Part of that is education, and this book is part of it, combining the operating patterns you already run with those of software companies.

## The Headcount *Paradox*.

Here is the math you're living right now.

The company is growing. The pipeline is healthy. So your leadership team is asking to hire. Another account manager. Another ops person. Another engineer. The assumption underneath is that growth means adding people. Automation is familiar in manufacturing, where machines replaced repetitive physical work. It's less familiar in the information economy, where the work requires judgment. And it's almost entirely unfamiliar in an intelligence economy, where decisions themselves can be assisted or handled by a non-human worker. When operators think about software here, they think about moving data between systems, maybe Zapier, maybe an integration. They aren't yet thinking about AI for work that requires decisions. But now they can.

You've bought some AI: a ChatGPT subscription, maybe an automation tool, maybe a consultant for a few hours. You didn't bet the farm. Most operators haven't. The spend has been small. You're willing to invest more. The budget is there. The intent is there. But you don't know where to aim, what to buy, what to build, or what return to expect.

Revenue and headcount run on a slope: every meaningful jump in revenue pulls a roughly proportional jump in headcount along with it. That slope was steep in 2022, and for most mid-market operators the AI line item on the P&L, small as it is, hasn't done anything to bend it. A handful of enterprises that have taken this work seriously are already seeing the slope start to flatten in specific functions. The pattern hasn't reached the middle market yet, which is who this book is for.

The slope has a name. Divide revenue by headcount and you get revenue per employee, the metric that sits under the paradox. In most companies it stays roughly flat as they grow: each new dollar of revenue arrives with about the same amount of human labor attached to it. Every company can calculate this number today. What this book is about is moving it.

Meanwhile your COO (Integrator if you run EOS) is on the calendar asking to approve the next two roles. The numbers in the request aren't unreasonable: the work is real, the team is stretched, the demand is there. You sign off, because the alternative is throttling growth. But you sign off knowing the AI investment was supposed to bend that slope by now, and you can't point to the reason it didn't.

The Headcount Paradox: each new dollar of revenue still demands roughly the same headcount it did before, even after you invested in AI to change that math. The investment is on the books, and it hasn't changed the structure.

### How the math finally moves.

Here's how it resolved at Jesse's company. SuperWebPros, his software development firm, went from thirteen people to eight. We mapped every function, identified what required human judgment and what didn't, built agent teams for rule-based work, and kept humans on work that required taste, relationships, and strategic decisions. Billings went up. Profitability went up.

Five people left the company. They weren't laid off in a single round, and we worked to place several of them well. But those five seats are gone, because the work they existed to do now runs on systems we designed. At Jesse's company the slope inverted. The more common version is less extreme and just as valuable: the team grows slower than the top line, so the marginal headcount per next dollar of revenue drops. That's the Headcount Math moving the way it's supposed to.

That same math can work at very different scales. When a global food safety company completed a Fortune 500 division acquisition, Julie was the CHRO overseeing the integration across 44 countries. The instinct in every integration conversation was to add HR business partners by region. The alternative was to redesign the operating model first — making a deliberate decision about which HR functions required local human judgment and which could run on a standardized system. The resulting global HR function served 44 countries with a smaller proportional team than the pre-acquisition domestic function had. Not because headcount was cut. Because the work was designed before it was staffed.

::: callout-tip
## Pro Tip
The Headcount Paradox doesn't break by adding AI to the existing org chart. It breaks by redesigning the org chart so AI has a seat on it. That's what changes the slope.
:::

{{< excalidraw ch01-headcount-before-after "The Headcount Paradox: the slope before redesign vs. the slope after — revenue climbs faster than headcount when work is designed before it's staffed." >}}

When AI investments don't pay off, the first instinct is to blame the tools — to assume the technology was oversold or that next quarter's version will finally do the thing. The tools are more capable than most operators realize. The problem is that there's no defined relationship between the AI system and the work it's supposed to do. There's no designed workflow, no clear accountability, and no governance. The tool sits in the background and helps individuals occasionally. It doesn't change the structure of the work. The math moves when the structure changes.

## It looks like a *technology* problem. It's actually an *operating* problem.

Your AI investments aren't producing returns because of an operating-model problem. Specifically, a Co-Intelligent Co-Operation problem.

A *Co-Intelligent Co-Operation problem* has two parts. *Co-Intelligent* is the actual workforce: humans and AI as one system, defined in Chapter 2. *Co-Operation* is the structural work of getting that workforce to operate together.

Culture matters: a team that resists change will stall any initiative. Training matters: people need to know what the tools can do. Tool selection matters: the wrong platform creates its own drag. These are all real, but the deeper problem is the operating model. The company was designed, deliberately or by drift, to be run by humans alone. You then introduced a second kind of worker, synthetic, capable, available, and dropped it next to the structure without changing the structure. The new worker has no seat, no accountability, and no defined handoff. So it produces nothing the organization can compound on. Culture, training, and tools are necessary. The missing piece is structural redesign.

This failure has the same shape across thirty years of operating-model changes, long before AI. ERP rollouts are the clearest example: companies spent eight-figure sums to install new systems, then left the old reporting structures and decision rights exactly as they were. The system sat live while people worked around it. The pattern isn't that the technology failed. The capability arrived and the structure never changed to receive it. The new thing sat next to the old structure and produced nothing structural. AI is the latest technology to run into the same wall — the only difference is the speed and cost of the collision.

AI is usually treated as a chatbot — a thing you type questions into and read answers from. In most companies, that's the relationship: one human, one chat window, one task at a time. Every instruction comes from the human, and every output goes back to the human. That can raise productivity, but it doesn't compound, because the human is still the bottleneck.

The real capability is in agents — the kind defined earlier: workflows that take actions and run steps on their own, where the design says which moves require a human review and which don't. An agent can research, draft, route, check, escalate, and deliver inside a designed system. And agents can run in parallel. While you're reviewing one deliverable, three other workstreams are moving.

EOS, Scaling Up, and other disciplined systems are built on this shape: an Accountability Chart, scorecards, and the L10 (EOS's weekly leadership meeting) or its equivalent. Work added without a named owner dies in the gap. AI is no different. It's a new kind of worker added to the system without anyone naming who owns it, what it's accountable for, or where the handoffs live. So it dies in the gap, the same way any unowned function does.

Walk into any function in your company today and ask the same three questions you'd ask of a human team: what is this function accountable for, what is its scorecard, who reviews the output and on what cadence. The humans have answers. The AI doesn't. The AI in your company has no seat on the chart, no number it's hitting, and no review rhythm. You wouldn't run a function staffed by people that way. The AI isn't being treated as staff.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

Walk into your next L10 or leadership meeting with this question: "If AI were an employee, what would its scorecard say?" Write down whatever the room produces. If the room can't answer — if there's no scorecard, no number, no owner — that's your answer. There is no scorecard. And that's exactly the problem.
:::

> The instinct to solve a people problem with another person is exactly the instinct this book exists to interrupt.

None of this is mysterious. All of it is operating work, not technology work. The frame is the operating model itself.

## The wrong *question*.

Every organization falls into the same trap at the start of its AI effort.

The first question most teams ask is task-oriented: *which of our existing tasks could AI help with?* It gets you some of the way there. You'll find prompt tips, a few useful shortcuts, some real time saved. Using AI to write a social media post is a fine task. But task-orientation is insufficient. It adds AI on top of the existing workflow, and that workflow was designed for humans. The gains stay small and scattered, and nothing changes structurally.

Companies that get this right end up with the Headcount Math working in their favor. Revenue and profitability climb while the team's growth rate decouples from the top line. The discipline behind that result is straightforward: start with the outcome the organization is accountable for, then design the work backward from that outcome. A single question drives the whole exercise: who owns what step, and does that step require judgment or follow a rule? The answer tells you where AI belongs and where it doesn't. Skipping the outcome and design steps and going straight to tools is what produces the scattered use cases and the stalled pilots. This discipline predates AI. The AI era made the cost of skipping it visible.

The question that unlocks real value is goal-oriented: *what outcomes are we accountable for, and how should the human + AI workforce be designed to deliver them?* That question starts with the outcomes and with accountability for them, not with the tools. It produces a deliberate design that sets who owns what, what the human reviews, what the agent team executes, where the handoff lives, and how the result gets measured. Writing a social post is a task. Building a content production workflow that holds up regardless of who's sitting in the seat is a bigger problem with a much bigger payoff.

::: callout-tip
## Pro Tip

If your AI initiative starts with "what tasks can AI do?" you'll get a list of tasks. If it starts with "what outcomes do we need, and who — human or AI — should own each one?" you'll get an operating model.
:::

{{< excalidraw ch01-wrong-vs-right-question "The Wrong Question vs. The Right Question" >}}

## Where you actually *stand*.

The AI Readiness Scorecard tells you where you stand.

The scorecard covers five dimensions of operational readiness, four questions per dimension, twenty questions in total. For each statement, rank your business 1 to 5, where 1 is weak and 5 is strong. At the end you'll add up the rankings, divide by 100, and turn the result into a percentage. That percentage places you on the AI divide we named earlier in this chapter.

Do this with whoever would be in the room if you were deciding whether to invest in AI. Not just you, the team.

A note before you start: you may not be able to answer all twenty questions cleanly. The scorecard shows you where you're starting. A low score is the starting point most companies are at, and the rest of this book is built to move you forward from there.

We'll define every term as we go. For now, a "constraint" means the one operational pain point your company keeps hitting: the thing your team keeps circling in meetings, the process that breaks when one person is out, the workflow where you feel the drag every week. Sometimes that pain is the biggest dollar cost on the P&L. Often it isn't. It might be the risk that keeps you up at night, the bottleneck that caps growth in a key account, the dependency on one person that you can't afford to lose. The cost matters and we'll get to the math in Dimension 5. The pain is what tells you where to look first.

The five dimensions sit inside two preconditions. Information Readiness and Workflow Visibility are the *technical preconditions* that determine whether an AI agent can actually do the work: whether the knowledge exists in a form the system can reach, and whether the workflow is mapped clearly enough to be handed off. Constraint Clarity, Decision Rights, and Measurement Discipline are the *operating-model preconditions* that determine whether your organization will hold the change once it's deployed: whether your team agrees on what to solve, who decides what AI touches, and whether you can measure the result. A company can score strongly on the technical side and weakly on the operating side, or the reverse. Both halves have to come up before a Sprint will hold.

### Dimension 1: Constraint Clarity

*Can your leadership team name the ONE operational constraint AI should solve?*

| # | Statement | 1–5 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | We can name one operational constraint that, if removed, would change next quarter's P&L. | ___ |
| 2 | We've quantified the cost of that constraint in dollars, hours, or margin. | ___ |
| 3 | Our leadership team agrees on what the #1 constraint actually is, not just that one exists. | ___ |
| 4 | We've traced the symptoms of the constraint back to a structural root. | ___ |

::: callout-note
## Action Step

Don't ask your leadership team what AI should solve. They don't know yet, and neither did you before you picked up this book. Ask them a question they *can* answer: "What is the one operational problem we keep circling and never close, the one that hurts the most, whether it shows up in dollars, hours, risk, or a person we can't afford to lose?" Poll each person individually, write down the answers verbatim, and compare. If five people give five different answers, you've found something more useful than a constraint. You've found the leadership-team disagreement that any AI work would have run into anyway.
:::

The poll results tell you more than any scorecard row. Agreement on the operational pain means you've got a starting point. Disagreement means the constraint isn't the workflow yet; it's the leadership team's agreement on what matters most.

::: callout-tip
## Pro Tip

If your leadership team can't agree on the constraint, that disagreement IS the diagnosis. No AI tool fixes misaligned priorities.
:::

### Dimension 2: Information Readiness

*Is the knowledge your team runs on documented and accessible, or trapped in people's heads?*

| # | Statement | 1–5 |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | We can answer "where does this information live?" for every critical workflow. | ___ |
| 6 | We've identified the institutional knowledge that exists only in one person's head. | ___ |
| 7 | The knowledge our team runs on is captured outside of conversations and email threads. | ___ |
| 8 | We have a process for keeping that knowledge current as the business changes. | ___ |

If your best operations person quit tomorrow, how long before the replacement could run the workflow without calling them? If the answer is "months," your real score is a 1 or a 2, regardless of what's in your wiki.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

Pick your most critical workflow. Ask the person who owns it: "If you had to hand this off to someone new on Monday, what would you give them?" Whatever they describe is the actual state of your documentation — not whatever lives in SharePoint.
:::

### Dimension 3: Workflow Visibility

*Can you draw the workflow where the constraint lives, including who does what and where handoffs break?*

| # | Statement | 1–5 |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | We can describe end-to-end how work moves through our critical processes. | ___ |
| 10 | We know where work currently breaks: manual handoffs, system gaps, undocumented expertise. | ___ |
| 11 | Our processes are documented at the task level, not just summarized. | ___ |
| 12 | We've identified which steps are routing and admin versus which require human judgment. | ___ |

A workflow described by one person isn't enough. The team has to agree on the map, and that's what AI needs to run on.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

Whiteboard your most constrained workflow in fifteen minutes. Put every handoff on the board. Circle the ones where work stalls, errors appear, or people say "I'll just handle it myself." Those circles are where the real problem lives.
:::

### Dimension 4: Decision Rights

Your team needs to know who decides what AI handles and what stays with humans.

| # | Statement | 1–5 |
|---|---|---|
| 13 | Every accountability in our org has exactly one named owner. | ___ |
| 14 | We've documented which decisions require human review and which can run inside a designed scope. | ___ |
| 15 | When a workflow fails, we can name who's accountable without ambiguity. | ___ |
| 16 | Our team agrees on who has the authority to change the boundary between human work and AI work. | ___ |

Decision rights come down to organizational trust, not AI capability. The question is whether you trust the output enough to act on it without a human checking. That's a leadership decision. And not every workflow should aim for full automation. Some workflows should keep a human in the loop. Make that a deliberate choice based on the goal, not a default because nobody designed the alternative.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

List the five most frequent decisions in your constrained workflow. For each one, write down who currently makes the decision and whether it requires judgment or just follows a rule. The rule-based ones are AI-eligible. The judgment ones need a human-in-the-loop design.
:::

### Dimension 5: Measurement Discipline

*Can you put a dollar number on what the constraint costs per quarter?*

| # | Statement | 1–5 |
|---|---|---|
| 17 | We measure outcomes weekly with named numbers, not vibes. | ___ |
| 18 | Every team has a scorecard with five to fifteen metrics they own. | ___ |
| 19 | We can prove last quarter's investments paid back, in dollars. | ___ |
| 20 | We track revenue per employee and review it at least quarterly. | ___ |

If you can't measure what the constraint costs today, you can't measure whether AI made it better tomorrow. Cost here is broader than dollars. It can be hours lost, deals walked, errors caught late, customers who churned quietly, the risk you carry in one person's head. Dollar cost is the cleanest version, and where you can get to it, use it. Where you can't, pick the most honest unit you can defend and measure it the same way every quarter. Without that, you have an AI experiment, not an AI initiative. An initiative has a target.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

Do the math right now. Hours per week spent on the constraint, multiplied by loaded cost per hour, multiplied by thirteen weeks. That's your quarterly cost floor. If you can't fill in the numbers, write down what data you'd need and where you'd get it. That gap is your first task.
:::

### Score yourself.

For each of the twenty statements above, you ranked your business 1 to 5. Now tally the count of each ranking across all twenty rows.

| Count of each ranking | ___ ones | ___ twos | ___ threes | ___ fours | ___ fives |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Multiply by | × 1 | × 2 | × 3 | × 4 | × 5 |
| Subtotal | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ |

Add the five subtotals together. The lowest possible total is 20 (every row scored 1). The highest is 100 (every row scored 5). Your total is your AI Readiness percentage: ___%.

### Read your bucket.

| Score | What it means |
|---|---|
| **20–34%** | Start here. This book is for you. The operating model isn't designed for AI yet, the basic preconditions aren't in place, and that is the most honest answer most mid-market companies give on first read. |
| **35–49%** | Foundations exist. The math hasn't compounded yet. Most readers land here. You have partial answers across most dimensions; the work is locking the answers, not inventing them. |
| **50–64%** | You're above average. The framework will sharpen what's already there. Expect faster movement in two or three dimensions and slower work in whichever one you scored lowest. |
| **65–79%** | You're operating well. The book formalizes what you already do informally and gives you the language to scale the discipline beyond the people who currently carry it. |
| **80–100%** | You're running a Co-Intelligent Co-Operation in fact, if not in name. The chapters ahead will give you the vocabulary, the artifacts, and the through-line to make what you've built repeatable across the next decade of growth. |

Look at the dimensions inside the score. Add the four rankings inside each dimension to get a dimension subtotal out of 20. The dimension with the lowest subtotal is where the chapters ahead start moving the math for you.

::: callout-note
## Your closing checklist

Before you turn the page, write these four numbers down:

- **Your overall AI Readiness score:** ____ %
- **Your lowest dimension(s):** _______________
- **Your highest dimension(s):** _______________
- **The dimension you'll start with:** _______________ (Chapter 5 hands you the rubric for choosing it on purpose, not by gut.)
:::

::: callout-tip
## Pro Tip

The scorecard isn't a test. It's a map of where to start. The lowest dimension is your first move. The highest is the foundation you protect while you do the work.
:::

Before we hand you the system, there are four things you have to be willing to believe.

## Reflection Questions

1.  Which of the five AI Readiness Scorecard dimensions scored lowest for your company, and does your leadership team agree on that score, or would each person give a different number?
2.  Walk into your next leadership meeting and ask: what is the one operational problem this company keeps circling and never closes? Write down the answers verbatim, one per person. How much do they overlap, and what does that overlap (or its absence) tell you about whether you've got a constraint problem or an agreement problem?
3.  Are you running the wrong question? When your team discusses AI, does the conversation start with "what tasks could AI help with?" or "what outcomes are we accountable for, and how should human + AI deliver them?" Which framing dominated your last AI conversation?
4.  The Headcount Paradox says revenue and headcount move on a slope, and AI was supposed to bend it. Pull your own numbers: what is your revenue per employee today versus two years ago? Has the AI line item moved that number at all?
5.  Describe your operating model in three sentences: how work actually moves through your company, not the org chart. If you can't do it in three sentences, what does that tell you about where AI would even plug in?
